analysis.one_liner: Replaces all public and private health insurance with a single government plan covering everyone with no copays or deductibles.
analysis.headline: Backed by 118 House Democrats, the bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a national health insurance program run by the Department of Health and Human Services that automatically covers every U.S. resident. It would pay for hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health and substance abuse treatment, dental, vision, and long-term care, with no deductibles, copays, or surprise balance bills. Private insurers could sell only supplemental coverage, not plans duplicating the public program, and the government would negotiate drug prices. Benefits would phase in over two years, with children, adults 55 and older, and current Medicare enrollees covered first.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of Americans who are uninsured, underinsured, or paying high premiums and deductibles would gain coverage with no out-of-pocket costs for covered care. People with employer insurance could stop depending on their job for health coverage. Displaced health insurance workers would receive wage replacement and retraining from a dedicated transition fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured, underinsured, and people with high deductibles

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. resident is automatically enrolled and entitled to comprehensive coverage, including hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health and substance abuse treatment, dental, vision, audiology, and long-term care services.

The bill bans all cost-sharing — deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments — and prohibits providers from balance-billing patients for covered services, eliminating out-of-pocket costs at the point of care.

Private health insurers and employers are barred from selling or providing coverage that duplicates the program's benefits, ending premium payments and job-based coverage dependence; insurers may sell only supplemental benefits.

The Department of Health and Human Services must negotiate prescription drug prices, and provider payments are set through global budgets and a national fee schedule instead of negotiated private rates.
Coverage would phase in over two years: children under 19, adults 55 and older, and current Medicare enrollees could enroll one year after enactment, with a transitional buy-in option.

Up to 1 percent of the health budget for five years is reserved to assist workers displaced from health insurance administration and related jobs, including wage replacement, retirement benefits, and retraining.

analysis.who_pays: The bill as written contains no financing provisions, so the tax burden for the program is not specified in the text. By design, the cost of paying for everyone's care shifts to the federal budget. Hospitals and doctors would face payment rates based on Medicare rates rather than higher private-insurance rates, and drug makers would take lower prices from government negotiation. Roughly 500,000-plus health insurance industry workers would need retraining, cushioned by the transition fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, hospitals, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The bill text contains no financing provisions — no taxes or funding mechanism are specified — so the total cost and who would pay for it are left entirely to future legislation.

Everyone with job-based coverage, ACA exchange plans, Medicare Advantage, or private insurance would lose that coverage when the program phases in, even if they like their current plan, because duplicating coverage becomes unlawful.

Hospital and doctor payments would be set from Medicare operating rates, excluding value-based and capital payment adjustments, which are lower than the rates private insurers currently pay; the bill does not spell out how a funding shortfall or capacity strain would be resolved.
Adding long-term care coverage for all enrollees is a major new entitlement with no dedicated revenue in the bill, making the program's long-term solvency dependent on future Congresses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its face, the bill trades everyone's premiums, deductibles, and copays for a single public plan — a large gain for households against medical debt and coverage gaps, and a large cost shift onto the federal budget. The bill's central weakness is that it specifies the benefits without specifying the financing: an honest supporter would acknowledge that the plan's real cost, and the taxes needed to fund it, are unknown as written. The two-year phase-in and the transition fund for insurance workers soften the disruption but do not answer the funding question.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in six House committees for nearly the entire Congress, got a single subcommittee hearing, and never reached a committee vote or the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Medicare for All Act of 2019 on February 27, 2019, and it was referred to six House committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Rules, Oversight and Reform, and Armed Services.
118 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.
In nearly two years, the only action after referral was one Health Subcommittee hearing on December 10, 2019; no committee reported the bill and no floor vote ever occurred.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with the bill still pending in committee, so it died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and employers kept the existing insurance system and avoided the taxes that would have funded the program. House leaders also avoided forcing members to cast a recorded vote on a major health care overhaul. People without coverage or with high deductibles gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, drug makers, and House Democratic leaders

sides.party_line_note: All 118 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; because the bill never got a vote, the chamber's recorded position was its referral rather than any roll call.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to sell coverage duplicating the public plan and sunsets the ACA exchanges, shrinking the industry to supplemental-only products. It is the largest loser in the bill: its core business of paying for basic care would be replaced by a government program.

The bill requires HHS to negotiate prescription drug prices, replacing the current system where manufacturers set prices against private insurers. Lower drug prices directly cut the industry's revenue.

Hospitals would gain guaranteed payment, global budgets covering operating costs, and the end of unpaid care and billing costs — but their payments would be set off Medicare operating rates, which are below private-insurance rates. Industry groups opposed the bill in the 2019-2020 debate.

The bill prohibits employers from providing coverage that duplicates the public program, which would free them from today's multi-thousand-dollar-per-worker premiums but shift the funding obligation to taxes that would fall partly on business. Workers would gain coverage independent of their job.

industries.industry: Medical billing, claims administration, and insurance intermediaries
industries.note: A single payer running claims through HHS eliminates much of the private claims-processing and prior-authorization industry. The bill's transition fund covers some displaced workers for up to five years.
